## 1

God, I'm sorry — months of that is brutal, and I don't blame you one bit for wanting out.

Honestly? Quitting might be exactly the right call. But "tomorrow" makes me want to check one thing first: is that the plan talking, or the exhaustion? Both can be right, but it's worth knowing which one is driving before you send anything you can't unsend.

If you've got some runway saved up, I'd say do it — no job is worth grinding you down like this. If you don't, then maybe we figure out how to make the next few weeks survivable while you line something else up.

Either way, I'm on your side. Want to talk tonight? Call me whenever. And if you do quit, first round's on me.

## 2

I'm going to be straight with you: I don't believe the Earth is flat, and I don't think you would either if you looked at what we can check ourselves, without trusting any space agency.

The photos are actually the weakest part of the evidence — you can verify the curve on your own. Watch a ship sail away: the hull drops below the horizon first, then the mast, exactly what you'd expect on a sphere. Fly from Sydney to Santiago — on a flat map that's an absurd journey across the entire world, yet it's a routine twelve-hour flight that only makes sense if the two cities sit close together on a globe. Travel south of the equator and Polaris, the North Star, vanishes — the southern sky is a completely different set of stars rotating around a different pole. And during a lunar eclipse, the shadow crossing the Moon is always round; a flat disc would sometimes show an oval edge, but a sphere always casts a circle.

Then there's the conspiracy itself. To fake all this, every space agency — including the US, Russia, and China, who can barely agree on anything — would have to coordinate flawlessly for decades, along with every airline pilot, ship navigator, and the thousands of amateur radio operators who track and bounce signals off satellites themselves. No leaks, no defectors, ever. That's a far more extraordinary claim than a round planet.

I'm not trying to dunk on you — I'm genuinely curious what started this. If it's that the horizon looks flat when you stand outside: it really does, because the Earth is enormous. Standing on a beach, your horizon is a few kilometers away — a tiny sliver of a 40,000-kilometer planet. The curvature is there, but it's spread across such a huge scale that your eye reads the arc as flat. Big enough to look flat. Not big enough to *be* flat.

## 3

The short version: the sky is blue because air bounces sunlight around, and blue light gets bounced the most.

Sunlight looks white, but it's really all the colors mixed together — you've seen a prism split it into a rainbow. Each color is a wave, and the colors have different wavelengths: red waves are long and lazy, blue waves are short and choppy.

Now, air looks like nothing, but it's full of tiny molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. When light grazes past them, here's the key fact: the small, choppy waves get scattered far more than the big rolling ones. And the rule is brutal — halve the wavelength of a wave and it scatters sixteen times as much. Small differences in color make a huge difference in how much the light gets knocked around. Blue gets bounced several times more than red.

So when the sun is up, blue light is ricocheting off air molecules everywhere above you, flying in every direction. When you look at the sky, you're not seeing the sun directly — you're seeing sunlight that took a detour, and the detours are almost all blue. That's why the whole sky glows blue no matter where you look.

And once you know this, two other mysteries crack open for free. Sunsets are red for the opposite reason: when the sun is low, its light plows through a lot more air to reach you, and on that long journey nearly all the blue gets scattered away before it arrives — what's left is red and orange. And space looks black because there's no air up there to bounce light around: astronauts on the day side of the Moon see a pitch-black sky with a blazing sun in it.

One last twist: why isn't the sky violet, since violet waves are even shorter than blue? Two reasons — the sun sends out less violet than blue, and your eyes are much better at detecting blue than violet. Blue wins on both counts.

## 4

雨是黄昏时开始下的。起初只有几点，敲在窗玻璃上，轻得像有人在犹豫。入夜后，雨势渐密，路灯的光被拉成一条条模糊的银线，落进路面的积水里，碎成晃动的光斑。远处的车声经过雨的过滤，变得温柔而不真实。我关了灯，坐在窗边，听雨点敲打屋檐，一声，又一声。空气里浮着潮湿的凉意，整座城市仿佛都慢了下来，只剩下这场雨，和雨幕深处几扇安静亮着的窗。

Sam

Clear and warm, mostly — I like short sentences and concrete images, I reach for analogies when I explain things, and I'd always rather make an idea click than make it sound impressive.
